The aim was to characterize CP-E. coli isolates recovered from Slovenian patients between 1 January and 31 December 2023 using whole-genome sequencing (WGS), providing a national snapshot of the population structure and circulating strains.
Methods: WGS was performed using short-read sequencing. Bioinformatic analyses included identification of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants, multilocus sequence typing (MLST), phylogroup typing, core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST), assessment of genetic relatedness, and plasmid reconstruction using MOB-suite.
Results: A total of 108 CP-E. coli isolates (108 patients) were included. Most isolates originated from surveillance samples (89.8%), 30.6% were detected more than 48 h after hospital admission. OXA-48-like carbapenemases predominated (70.4%), followed by metallo-β-lactamases (29.6%), with OXA-48 (44.4%), OXA-244 (22.2%), and VIM-1 (18.5%) being the most common enzymes. Despite carbapenemase production, 69.4% of isolates remained phenotypically susceptible to carbapenems. WGS revealed substantial genetic diversity, with 67 sequence types (STs) identified among 108 isolates. The most common lineages were ST10 (13.9%), ST38 (12.0%), ST5295 (9.3%), and ST69 (6.5%). Phylogroup A was the most prevalent, followed by D, B2, and B1. cgMLST analysis identified six transmission clusters comprising 26 isolates (24.1%), the remaining isolates were sporadic. Plasmid analysis based on short-read sequencing demonstrated extensive horizontal dissemination of carbapenemase genes, with blaOXA-48 predominantly associated with IncL/M plasmids and blaVIM-1 with IncA plasmids. Closely related plasmids were detected across multiple genetically distinct STs, indicating widespread plasmid-mediated transmission.
Discussion: CP-E. coli in Slovenia is characterized by a rising burden, high genetic diversity, and a predominance of OXA-48-like carbapenemases. While limited clonal transmission was observed, the widespread distribution of closely related carbapenemase-carrying plasmids across diverse sequence types indicates that horizontal plasmid transfer is the principal driver of dissemination. These findings highlight the value of the national genomic surveillance for monitoring both clonal spread and plasmid-mediated transmission of carbapenem resistance.

title: Prospective Molecular and Phenotypic Characterization of blaCTX-M and blaTEM ESBL Genes in Uropathogenic Escherichia coli from ICU Patients at Three Tertiary-Care Hospitals in Tabriz, Iran.
abstract:
Background: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) caused by extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli have become a major therapeutic challenge worldwide, especially in intensive care units. In northwestern Iran, the molecular epidemiology of the key resistance genes blaCTX-M and blaTEM, along with their potential co-carriage on plasmids, remains poorly understood. This gap limits the development of effective local empirical treatment guidelines and infection control strategies.
Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted at three tertiary-care hospitals in Tabriz, Iran (2025). We identified 100 non-duplicate Escherichia coli isolates recovered from ICU patients with UTIs using standard microbiological methods. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by the disk diffusion method according to CLSI 2024 guidelines. ESBL phenotype was confirmed using the combined disk test with Ceftazidime and Clavulanic acid. Genotypic detection of blaTEM and blaCTX-M was performed by conventional PCR. Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests were used to assess statistical associations.
Results: Among 135 culture-positive urine specimens, E. coli was the predominant pathogen (74.07%), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae (11.85%). Universal resistance to Cefotaxime (100%) and high resistance to Ceftazidime (95%) were observed. Imipenem retained the highest in vitro activity (82% susceptibility). Phenotypic ESBL production was detected in 48/100 (48%) isolates. Among ESBL producers, blaTEM was present in 28 (58.3%), blaCTX-M in 20 (41.7%), and both genes co-occurred in 18 isolates (37.5%). The observed co-occurrence significantly exceeded expected values under independence (observed: 18 vs. expected: 11.7; Chi-square p = 0.0005; Fisher's exact p = 0.00025), demonstrating non-random co-occurrence consistent with, but not proof of, plasmid-mediated co-carriage.
Conclusion: ESBL-producing E. coli carrying both blaTEM and blaCTX-M are highly prevalent among ICU-associated UTI in Tabriz. The statistically significant non-random co-occurrence of these genes has direct implications for surveillance strategies, necessitating simultaneous genotyping of both genes. Carbapenems remain effective, underscoring the urgency of their stewardship to prevent the emergence of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) in this setting.

title: Genomic insights into carbapenemase- and extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing gram-negative bacteria in aquatic and terrestrial animal reservoirs in the United Arab Emirates.
abstract:
Background: The global spread of carbapenemase- and extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Gram-negative bacteria represents a major One Health challenge, driven by interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs. However, genomic data on antimicrobial-resistant bacteria associated with aquatic and terrestrial animals in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) remain scarce, limiting assessment of their potential role in resistance dissemination. This study investigated the phenotypic and genomic characteristics of resistant Gram-negative bacteria recovered from these animal reservoirs.
Methods: Sixty aquarium-associated samples were collected, yielding 69 Gram-negative isolates. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing, phenotypic detection of ESBL and carbapenemase activity, molecular screening of resistance genes, and whole-genome sequencing of selected isolates were performed. Phylogenetic analyses were conducted to assess evolutionary relatedness with global strains.
Results: The isolates were mainly identified as Citrobacter, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, and Escherichia coli. Resistance to β-lactam antibiotics was widespread, with 87% of isolates confirmed as ESBL producers and 37.7% classified as multidrug resistant. Carbapenemase activity was detected in 14.5% of isolates. Genomic analyses revealed diverse ESBL, AmpC, and carbapenemase genes, including bla CTX-M-15, bla CTX-M-55, bla CMY-82, bla NDM-1, and for the first time multiple OXA-type carbapenemases (bla OXA-51, bla OXA-421, and bla OXA-848, bla OXA-1005, bla OXA-211-like, and bla OXA-396-like), frequently associated with mobile genetic elements. ESBL-producing E. coli ST602 and ST10 clustered closely with human, food, wildlife, and environmental strains from national and international sources.
Conclusion: Aquatic and terrestrial animals in the UAE serve as important reservoirs for clinically relevant antimicrobial resistance. These findings underscore the need for integrated One Health genomic surveillance to mitigate the transboundary spread of high-risk resistant lineages.

title: Discovery of bacterial biofilm inhibitors against catheter-associated urinary tract infections using computational approaches.
abstract: One of the most frequent device-associated infections obtained in a hospital setting is catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI). The rise of CAUTIs caused by biofilm-forming bacteria, including Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Enterococcus faecalis, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus, has become a significant challenge due to their drug resistance phenomenon in healthcare settings. Biofilms confer resistance to both host immune responses and antimicrobial drugs, making infections difficult to treat. This review aims to explore biofilm inhibitors targeting proteins that have not yet been fully explored computationally against CAUTI-causing bacteria, and to examine the molecular mechanisms of biofilm formation in the six major bacteria. A list of potential inhibitors from both natural and synthetic sources, identified through computational approaches by various groups, has been mentioned for further research in in vitro and in vivo models. In addition, there is a considerable scope of artificial intelligence and machine learning, which has been highlighted to overcome the challenges and limitations of current states of promising inhibitor development, as well as a description of future directions for computational methods against CAUTI-associated bacterial biofilm-mediated drug resistance has been included to sort out the current limitations.

title: Synthesis and Antibacterial Assessment of Novel Azithromycin Derivatives as Potential Taste-Masking Prodrugs.
abstract: <b>Background and Objective:</b> Azithromycin is a widely used macrolide antibiotic with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical acceptability is limited by poor patient compliance due to its bitter taste. Additionally, the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance necessitates the development of novel derivatives with improved therapeutic performance. This study aimed to synthesize and evaluate novel azithromycin derivatives with dual potential for taste masking and enhanced antibacterial activity. <b>Materials and Methods:</b> Five novel azithromycin derivatives were synthesized by reacting azithromycin with different functional linkers, including <i>N</i>-acetyl benzenesulfonyl chloride, <i>p</i>-nitrobenzoyl chloride, <i>p</i>-toluenesulfonyl chloride, 3,5-dinitrobenzoyl chloride and <i>p</i>-nitrobenzenesulfonyl chloride. The synthesized compounds were characterized using Fourier-Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FT-IR), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and mass spectrometry (MS). Prodrug properties were assessed through kinetic stability studies at physiological pH values (2.2, 5.5 and 7.4). Antibacterial activity was evaluated <i>in-vitro</i> using minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and Half-Maximal Inhibitory Concentration (IC<sub>50</sub>) assays against clinically relevant bacterial strains, including <i>Escherichia coli</i>, <i>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</i>, <i>Streptococcus pneumoniae</i> and <i>Staphylococcus aureus</i>. The bacterial strains used in this study were standard ATCC reference strains and were not derived from human or animal subjects. Therefore, ethical approval was not required. All experiments were conducted following standard microbiological laboratory practices. <b>Results:</b> All five azithromycin derivatives were successfully synthesized with satisfactory yields and confirmed structural characteristics. <strong>Compounds 2, 4 and 5</strong> demonstrated favorable prodrug behavior by undergoing pH-dependent hydrolysis and regenerating the parent drug, indicating promising taste-masking potential. Furthermore, <strong>compounds 1 and 3</strong> exhibited superior antibacterial activity against <i>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</i> compared to the parent azithromycin. <b>Conclusion:</b> The synthesized azithromycin derivatives demonstrated promising potential as next-generation therapeutic agents with improved palatability and retained or enhanced antimicrobial efficacy. These findings support their prospective application in overcoming taste-related compliance issues while addressing antimicrobial resistance challenges.
journal: Pakistan journal of biological sciences : PJBS

title: Genomic prediction of antimicrobial resistance in priority healthcare pathogens using Staramr.
abstract:
Unlabelled: Treatment of healthcare-associated infections is becoming increasingly challenging due to rising antimicrobial resistance (AMR). As clinical microbiology and public health continue to transition toward whole-genome sequencing (WGS) for outbreak detection, diagnostics, and surveillance, the ability to accurately predict antimicrobial resistance from genomic sequence data will become crucial. In this study, in silico antimicrobial resistance prediction with the Staramr tool was refined from whole-genome sequencing data for four top-priority healthcare-associated bacteria: carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli, carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium. Isolates (n = 4,876) were collected in Canada within two national surveillance programs: the Canadian Nosocomial Infection Surveillance Program and the Canadian Ward Study. Broth microdilution was used as the gold standard to evaluate the performance of Staramr. The average sensitivity, specificity, and concordance of categorical antimicrobial resistance prediction compared to broth microdilution were 90.8%, 90.1%, and 92.4% for E. coli (n = 1,095); 87.7%, 91.7%, and 90.6% for K. pneumoniae (n = 687); 95.5%, 98.9%, and 96.3% for methicillin-resistant S. aureus (n = 2,150); and 95.4%, 97.9%, and 97.2% for vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (n = 944). Additionally, this internal tool refinement identified areas of improvement for antimicrobial resistance prediction. The average sensitivity, specificity, and concordance of antimicrobial resistance prediction were high (>90%) for most combinations of antimicrobials and species that were evaluated. While AMR prediction from WGS was very promising, it did not correlate well with current Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute breakpoints for non-susceptibility for some antimicrobial-organism combinations. As in silico prediction of antimicrobial resistance has been improved in this study through tool refinement, it shows future promise for molecular methods to complement phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing. This will allow for more precise tracking of the molecular epidemiology of resistance and cost savings when isolates are being sequenced for strain typing.
Importance: In silico prediction of antimicrobial non-susceptibility in priority healthcare pathogens is becoming an important area of study due to the rising rates of resistance and the transition to whole-genome sequencing. To evaluate whether Staramr, an antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prediction tool, can reliably detect non-susceptibility in four top-priority healthcare-associated bacteria, we performed a validation study on a large Canadian clinical data set, which included carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus. Compared to traditional antimicrobial susceptibility testing, we found that Staramr was reliable for predicting non-susceptibility for most combinations of antimicrobials and organisms; however, some combinations require additional data on genetic mechanisms of resistance for accurate prediction. Additionally, this study identified areas for refinement for current drug-gene interpretation keys. Thus, this tool refinement study advances the use of genotypic methods of AMR prediction for high-priority healthcare pathogens.

title: Comparative antibacterial, synergistic, and anti-biofilm efficacy of metal ions against multidrug-resistant pathogens on dairy equipment surfaces.
abstract:
Unlabelled: This study evaluated the antibacterial and anti-biofilm activities of selected metal ions (Al3+, Cu2+, Au3+, Ag+, and Zn2+) against extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-E. coli), Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecalis (VRE). The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified the threat posed by multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens, particularly biofilm-forming bacteria associated with dairy equipment surfaces. Among the tested metals, silver ions showed the strongest antibacterial activity, producing inhibition zones up to 19.00 ± 1.15 mm at 0.3125 mM and a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 0.078 mM, followed by gold ions (MIC 2.5 mM). Zinc and copper exhibited moderate activity at higher concentrations, whereas aluminium showed the least effect. Checkerboard assays demonstrated synergistic or additive interactions, particularly for Cu-Au, Zn-Cu, and Zn-Ag combinations [Fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) 0.5-0.75], while a ternary Cu-Zn-Ag combination showed notable additive interaction (FICI 0.512). Propidium iodide uptake assays suggested membrane damage and disruption of cell integrity. Silver also exhibited the highest biofilm eradication activity (50% biofilm eradication concentration (BEC₅₀ 0.156 mM), followed by gold and copper. On stainless steel dairy equipment surfaces, silver and gold reduced biofilm biomass by > 60% and > 40%, respectively, as confirmed by confocal laser scanning microscopy and scanning electron microscopy. Silver additionally induced the highest intracellular reactive oxygen species generation (florescence intensity 93854.92 ± 2616.2 to 165407.18 ± 148.3), indicating oxidative stress-mediated antibacterial action than other metals. This study provides a comparative evaluation of metal ions and their synergistic combinations against MDR pathogens and biofilms associated with dairy equipment surfaces and dairy-processing environments.
Supplementary information: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05084-4.

title: Prevalence and antimicrobial resistance profiles of Campylobacter coli, Campylobacter jejuni, and Escherichia coli in the poultry distribution network.
abstract: India is one of the largest producers of poultry and poultry-derived products. The dynamics of animal production and consumer exposure have been linked to new challenges in the control of poultry-borne zoonotic diseases as consumption of poultry products raises. As a part of the One Health Poultry Hub, this study focused on addressing the risk posed by pathogens associated to the intensification of poultry production. Eight cities in the state of Gujarat were included in the study based on poultry density and distribution networks (PDN). Samples were collected from 65 live bird market shops and 50 poultry farms. The prevalence of key food borne pathogens - specifically Campylobacter spp. and Escherichia coli - was assessed using cecal and cloacal samples from birds, while non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) spp. was examined in environment samples from poultry farms. Campylobacter spp. and E. coli were recovered from 10.26% and 51.33% birds, respectively, whereas NTS spp. was not detected in any environmental sample. Prevalence pattern varied by city, season and breed. The highest C. coli prevalence was in broiler shop samples from Surat (17.5%) and desi chickens form Bhuj (16.7%), while C. jejuni peaked in broiler shop samples from Bhuj (13.3%). C. jejuni was not detected in desi chickens. All isolates were further analyzed for antimicrobial susceptibility and resistance using the disc diffusion method. A higher resistance was observed in Campylobacter isolates (55.74%) particularly against fluoroquinolones, macrolides and beta-lactams. Among the isolated organisms, 39.34% of Campylobacter and 61.03% of E. coli isolates exhibited extensively drug-resistant (XDR) phenotypes, while 4.92% of Campylobacter and 9.09% of E. coli demonstrated pan drug-resistant (PDR) phenotypes. Among Escherichia coli isolates, 29.87% exhibited resistance to glycopeptides, nitrofurantoin, macrolides, tetracycline, beta-lactams, and fluoroquinolones. These findings underscore the critical need for implementing farm hygiene practices to mitigate the risk of food borne pathogens and antimicrobial resistance within poultry distribution networks.

title: 18AA Reprograms the Pyruvate Cycle and Enhances Proton Motive Force to Potentiate Ceftazidime-Avibactam against Drug-Resistant Escherichia coli.
abstract: The rising threat of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae demands novel strategies to restore antibiotic efficacy. Here we show that compound amino acid injection (18AA), a clinically approved parenteral nutrition formulation, markedly potentiates ceftazidime-avibactam (CZA) against multidrug-resistant and carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli. Checkerboard and Bliss independence analyses demonstrated strong synergy. Time-kill kinetics confirmed dose-dependent bactericidal enhancement across susceptible, multidrug-resistant, and carbapenem-resistant strains. In a panel of 113 clinical isolates, the combination significantly improved population-based killing efficacy (KE50 and KE90) compared to CZA alone. Moreover, 18AA prolonged the post-antibiotic effect, reduced mutation frequency, and delayed resistance development during serial passage over 15 cycles. Untargeted metabolomics revealed that 18AA induces profound metabolic reprogramming, with robust activation of the pyruvate cycle as the most prominent signature common to all tested strains; key biomarkers pyruvate, ketoglutarate, and succinate were identified. Mechanistically, 18AA boosted the pyruvate cycle, increased NADH production, and elevated proton motive force (PMF), thereby promoting intracellular CZA accumulation, which was abrogated by the PMF uncoupler CCCP. Collectively, our findings establish 18AA as a promising metabolism-based adjuvant that rejuvenates CZA activity via the pyruvate cycle and PMF-dependent uptake, offering a readily translatable strategy against hard-to-treat E. coli infections.

title: Genomic characterization of bla NDM-5- and mcr-1-positive Escherichia coli from retail chicken meat reveals distinct plasmid organizations.
abstract: Carbapenems and polymyxins are critically important antimicrobial agents for treating severe infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. The global dissemination of the carbapenem resistance gene bla NDM and colistin resistance gene mcr-1 threatens the effectiveness of these last-line antibiotics. From a One Health perspective, food-producing animals and retail meat products may serve as reservoirs and vehicles for antimicrobial resistance determinants. This study investigated the occurrence and genomic characteristics of bla NDM-5- and mcr-1-coharboring Escherichia coli recovered from retail chicken meat to characterize their potential for dissemination through the food chain. Among 67 retail meat samples collected in Xuancheng, China, two meropenem-resistant E. coli isolates carrying both bla NDM-5 and mcr-1 were recovered exclusively from chicken meat. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing and hybrid whole-genome sequencing revealed that the isolates belonged to ST155 and ST165 and exhibited multidrug resistance. Phylogenetic analysis showed that both isolates were genetically distinct from global genomes of the same ST carrying bla NDM and/or mcr-1, suggesting that the two isolates were not derived from recent clonal dissemination represented in the analyzed dataset. Complete genome analysis identified two distinct plasmid organizations of bla NDM-5- and mcr-1: one isolate carried bla NDM-5 and mcr-1 on separate plasmids, whereas the other harbored both genes on a single conjugative IncHI2 plasmid. Comparative genomic analyses demonstrated high similarity between these plasmids and plasmids reported from humans, animals, and food sources. These findings highlight that poultry-associated E. coli may serve as carriers of important resistance determinants with potential for plasmid-mediated dissemination, emphasizing the need for integrated One Health genomic surveillance.

title: Occurrence of blaNDM-5 and blaNDM-29 variants and genetic diversity among Enterobacterales in hospitalized patients in northeastern Brazil : Variability of bla NDM in Enterobacterales.
abstract: This study investigated the genetic diversity and occurrence of blaNDM variants associated with carbapenem resistance in Enterobacterales obtained from colonization (rectal swabs) and infection sites in patients hospitalized in a public hospital in northeastern Brazil. A total of 58 multidrug-resistant clinical isolates were analyzed using ERIC-PCR to assess clonal relatedness, and PCR followed by amplicon sequencing to detect resistance genes (blaNDM, blaKPC, blaGES, blaVIM, and blaIMP). Klebsiella pneumoniae was the most frequently identified species (n = 28, 48.27%), followed by Serratia marcescens and Proteus mirabilis, among others. All seven P. mirabilis isolates were classified as XDR, as were six K. pneumoniae and three S. marcescens isolates. Amikacin (n = 46, 79.31% susceptible) and colistin (n = 37, 97.37% susceptible) exhibited the highest susceptibility rates among all antimicrobials tested against the majority of isolates. ERIC-PCR revealed multiclonal dissemination and high genetic variability among the isolates. The blaKPC gene was the most prevalent (n = 32, 55.17%), followed by blaNDM (n = 26, 44.83%). Among the blaNDM allelic variants, blaNDM-1 (n = 12, 46.15%) was the most common, followed by blaNDM-5 (n = 7, 26.92%) and blaNDM-29 (n = 1, 3.85%). This study reports the first detection in Brazil of blaNDM-5 in Klebsiella aerogenes, Citrobacter freundii, and Escherichia coli, in addition to reporting the first identification of blaNDM-29 in K. pneumoniae. Additionally, this study gives the first report in the Americas of blaNDM in Klebsiella ozaenae. These findings highlight the substantial potential for mutation and interspecies dissemination of blaNDM variants within the Enterobacterales order.
journal: Brazilian journal of microbiology : [publication of the Brazilian Society for Microbiology]

title: Emergence of blaOXA-244 in a single and dual-carbapenemase-producing clinical isolates of Escherichia coli from the United Arab Emirates.
abstract: ObjectivesCarbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales have emerged as a major global health concern owing to their rapid dissemination and limited therapeutic options. Here we report the first detection of blaOXA-244 in Escherichia coli from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and characterize two isolates genotypically and phenotypically, comparing them with geographically diverse public strains sharing the same sequence type (ST).MethodsThe isolates were recovered from the urine of a patient with metastatic cancer and from the abdominal fluid of a patient with sepsis. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing, including newer β-lactam and β-lactam/β-lactamase-inhibitors (BL/BLIs), and whole-genome sequencing were performed. Comparative genomic analysis was conducted against global and a defined Middle Eastern/North African subset matched by ST and carbapenemase profile.ResultsThe two isolates were genetically distinct: one carried blaOXA-244 alone and belonged to ST131, whereas the other harboured dual carbapenemases (blaOXA-244 and blaNDM-5) and belonged to ST361. Chromosomal location of blaOXA-244 was confirmed by Southern hybridization. Both isolates were multidrug-resistant, enriched with resistance genes spanning multiple antibiotic classes and virulence genes that support their pathogenicity. Phenotypically, the ST131 isolate remained susceptible to ceftazidime/avibactam and several BL/BLIs combinations, whereas the NDM-5-carrying ST361 isolate was resistant to ceftazidime/avibactam, cefepime/enmetazobactam, and cefepime/taniborbactam, highlighting the therapeutic challenge posed by metallo-β-lactamase co-production. Notably, both isolates remained susceptible to cefepime/zidebactam, cefiderocol, tigecycline, and colistin, and both showed low MICs for meropenem/xeruborbactam. The phylogenetic placement of both UAE isolates is consistent with membership in distinct carbapenem-resistant lineages detected across multiple countries; however, the routes of acquisition could not be inferred.ConclusionsThis is the first report of blaOXA-244 in E. coli from the UAE with two unrelated high-risk backgrounds. A dual OXA-244/NDM-5 ST361 lineage disseminated regionally since 2019 was identified. Because OXA-244 evades routine detection, genomic surveillance is needed to detect such emerging variants and to inform appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

title: Whole-Genome Sequencing-Based Characterization and Antimicrobial Resistance Analysis of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli Isolated from Retail Meat Products.
abstract: Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC), a zoonotic foodborne pathogen, has become a critical global public health issue. This study investigates molecular traits and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) mechanisms of STEC strains derived from retail meat products sourced from domestic production in Liaocheng city, Shandong province, China, to inform health risk assessment. Using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), phenotypic AMR testing, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS), 38 STEC isolates were identified from 400 retail meat products, with an isolation rate of 9.5%. Significant differences in STEC isolation rates were detected among different meat types, and mutton exhibited a relatively high isolation rate of 26.09%. Genomic virulence analysis showed that there were higher proportions of single stx2 (58.33%) and dual stx1/stx2 genotypes (33.33%) in mutton isolates than in beef (stx2: 48.00%, dual stx1/stx2: 12.00%), and only the stx2 gene was found in pork isolates. STEC isolates exhibited marked serotypic diversity, including O128ac:H2, O168:H7, O178:H7, O2:H25, and O6:H10. Multilocus sequence typing analysis revealed heterogeneous sequence type (ST) distributions among isolates, with ST10, ST25, and ST2722 as dominant STs, suggesting diverse contamination sources. STEC isolates exhibited high phenotypic resistance to tetracycline (TET) (68.42%), which corresponded to the highest detection rate of the TET resistance gene tet(A) at the genomic level. All isolates were susceptible to ertapenem, meropenem, ceftazidime, ceftazidime-avibactam, ciprofloxacin, and amikacin. Multidrug resistance (MDR) analysis indicated that 16 STEC isolates were MDR strains, with beef-derived isolates having relatively high MDR rates. This study verifies the occurrence of STEC in retail meat, highlighting prevalent AMR and substantial genetic heterogeneity among isolates. The findings underscore the necessity of systematic surveillance to limit STEC transmission along the meat supply chain and facilitate targeted food safety interventions.

title: Emergence and dissemination of an IncC plasmid co-harbouring bla KPC-2, bla NDM-1 and bla VIM-24 carbapenemase genes across multiple Gram-negative species in Colombia.
abstract:
Objectives: Carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacilli (CRGNB) pose a public health threat, increasingly driven by plasmid-mediated dissemination of carbapenemase genes. As part of a Colombian genomic monitoring programme, we aimed to characterize CRGNB co-harbouring multiple carbapenemase genes and determine their genetic context.
Methods: We screened 832 carbapenem-resistant isolates collected during 2011-2023 using carbapenemase-targeted qPCR. Ten isolates co-harbouring bla KPC, bla NDM and bla VIM underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing, long-read whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomics and conjugation assays.
Results: Nine Enterobacterales isolates and one Aeromonas caviae isolate from unrelated patients in geographically distant Colombian hospitals carried closely related IncC plasmids ranging from 160 to 317 kb. These plasmids co-harboured bla KPC-2, bla NDM-1 and bla VIM-24 within three conserved multidrug resistance regions, including a Tn21-associated region carrying bla NDM-1 and bla VIM-24 and a Tn6454-associated bla KPC-2 platform, alongside class 1 integrons, insertion sequences and multiple additional antimicrobial resistance determinants. The ten isolates were resistant to multiple β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations, and five were cefiderocol resistant. Aztreonam/avibactam remained active against all isolates; colistin resistance was confined to intrinsically resistant Providencia rettgeri and Serratia sarumanii. Conjugation assays demonstrated plasmid transfer to Escherichia coli J53, and sequencing confirmed transfer of a 179 kb IncC plasmid with functional conjugation machinery. Comparative genomic analysis showed a highly conserved IncC plasmid backbone across multiple species, supporting broad dissemination of this resistance platform.
Conclusions: This first report of a single plasmid co-harbouring three carbapenemase genes. This finding highlights a concerning mechanism for interspecies dissemination of MDR Gram-negative pathogens and underscores the importance of long-read genomic surveillance focused on high-risk plasmids.

title: Local temperature and humidity are associated with proportion of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli isolates in farm environments: considerations for on-farm surveillance.
abstract: Evidence suggests that increased local temperatures are associated with higher prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in environmental bacteria. This observational cohort study investigates associations between local climate and the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli isolated from 2,766 farm environment samples from 53 English dairy farms. A non-linear Bayesian model that accounts for decreased test sensitivity at low E. coli abundance was used to estimate the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli from colony count data. A 20°C increase in local temperature was associated with a 5.0-fold increase in the proportion of streptomycin-resistant E. coli (95% credible interval [CI]: 1.03-33.0; absolute increase: 0.2%, 95% CI: 2.3 × 10-3%-1.2%). Weaker evidence suggested that increased temperatures were associated with increased proportions of tetracycline-resistant E. coli. Increasing relative humidity was associated with an increase in the proportion of amoxicillin-, streptomycin-, and tetracycline-resistant E. coli. A 32% increase in relative humidity (from 60% to 92%) was associated with a 4.7-fold increase in the proportion of amoxicillin-resistant E. coli (median; 95% CI: 1.4-15.7; absolute increase: 1.3%, 95% CI: 0.2%-3.5%). For amoxicillin and streptomycin, a synergistic effect where increasing both temperature and humidity was associated with increased proportions of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli was observed, with weak evidence of this effect observed for tetracycline. These findings highlight the importance of considering weather conditions, sample characteristics, and seasonality in livestock AMR surveillance. Associations between local weather conditions and the proportion of livestock E. coli exhibiting AMR suggest that climate change may influence the burden of One Health AMR.IMPORTANCEUnderstanding how environmental conditions are associated with variability in antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence is critical for developing robust livestock AMR surveillance and anticipating the potential effects of climate change. The non-linear Bayesian modeling approach developed here adjusts for Escherichia coli abundance-associated variability in test sensitivity, enabling the influence of risk factors associated with the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli within samples to be more accurately estimated. Applying this approach to 2,766 fecal samples from 53 dairy farms in Southwest England indicated that the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli generally increased under warmer and wetter conditions. These findings suggest that environmental conditions can influence the prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant E. coli in dairy farm environments and demonstrate the importance of accounting for weather-related variability in livestock AMR surveillance. Adjusting for these associations in livestock AMR surveillance could improve the accuracy of modeling AMR trends and strengthen the assessment of climate-associated AMR risks.

title: Antimicrobial resistance patterns and difficult-to-treat resistance in uropathogens among diabetic and non-diabetic patients: a cross-sectional study.
abstract:
Background: While antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global challenge, data comparing Difficult-to-Treat Resistance (DTR) in diabetic versus non-diabetic urinary tract infection (UTI) patients is scarce. This study uniquely evaluates DTR and first-line resistance patterns to inform targeted empirical treatment strategies for these distinct patient cohorts.
Methods: A prospective observational cross-sectional study was conducted from August 2021 to January 2024, at a tertiary care teaching hospital in Vadodara, Gujarat, India. During the period, 2408 patients with symptoms of UTI were screened for urine culture and sensitivity, of which 954 individuals tested positive for UTIs.
Result: Of the 2,408 symptomatic patients screened, 954 (39.61%) tested positive. The within-group UTI positivity rate was 27.4% (280/1,023) among diabetic patients and 48.7% (674/1,385) among non-diabetic patients. Among the isolated uropathogens, Escherichia coli (E. coli) (56.78%, 62.90%) was the predominant organism followed by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) (13.57%, 5.78%) and Klebsiella spp. (13.21%, 17.35%) in diabetic and non-diabetic respectively. Among all the isolated uropathogen tetracycline (81.25%) and penicillin (71.86%) groups of antibiotics showed high resistance in diabetic patients, whereas fluoroquinolones had highest resistance in non-diabetic with 67.59%. However, the carbapenem, phosphonic and nitrofuran group of antibiotics showed least resistance in both diabetic and non-diabetic populations. Among all the antimicrobial drugs tested in our study, the first line of drugs was further analyzed, and P. aeruginosa had the highest DTR in both diabetic and non-diabetic individuals.
Conclusion: Despite lower culture positivity rates among diabetic patients, diabetic UTI cases demonstrated substantially higher AMR burden and DTR compared to non-diabetics. P. aeruginosa showed highest DTR prevalence. Penicillin and tetracycline resistance were markedly elevated in diabetic UTIs, while nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin maintained high effectiveness in both groups. These findings emphasize that diabetes is strongly associated with greater therapeutic complexity and multidrug resistance burden, necessitating resistance-guided empirical therapy and regional antibiogram surveillance for optimal UTI management.

title: Antibiotic susceptibility pattern of ESBLs-producing uropathogens in kidney transplant recipients in northern Iran.
abstract:
Background: Due to the increasing global prevalence of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing uropathogenic strains, ongoing surveillance is required to monitor drug-resistant organisms causing urinary tract infections (UTIs) in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs). This study aimed to evaluate the antibiotic resistance profiles of uropathogenic isolates in KTRs with UTIs caused by ESBL-producing strains.
Methods: A total of 96 urine samples collected from KTRs were cultured on selective media and analyzed using phenotypic characterization and PCR methods. Antibiotic resistance patterns among uropathogenic isolates were evaluated using the disk diffusion and E-test methods. Data were analyzed using SPSS Version 21, and the level of significance was set at 0.05.
Results: Among the 26 uropathogenic isolates, uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) was the most prevalent (15, 57.7%), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae (10, 38.5%) and Enterococcus faecalis (1, 3.8%). The rate of ESBL-producing isolates was 72% among UPEC and K. pneumoniae isolates. Antibiotic susceptibility testing revealed that ESBL-producing uropathogens exhibited significantly higher resistance rates (p < 0.05) than non-ESBL-producing strains to cefuroxime, cefepime, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin, and levofloxacin. E. faecalis showed susceptibility to vancomycin, penicillin, and ampicillin and resistance to ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin.
Conclusion: The rate of ESBL-related UTIs among KTRs was notable in this study. Based on the in vitro results, fosfomycin appears to be a promising oral therapeutic option for UTIs caused by ESBL-producing uropathogens in KTRs in the study region. In addition, the high prevalence of ESBL-producing isolates underscores the potential value of targeted prophylactic strategies for high-risk patients.

title: Co-occurrence of blaNDM-5 and mcr-1 on Two Distinct, Independently Transferable Plasmids in Commensal Escherichia coli ST156 from a Healthy Companion Dog.
abstract: The emergence of carbapenem- and colistin-resistant Enterobacterales mediated by transmissible plasmids poses a critical One Health threat by compromising the efficacy of last-resort antimicrobials. We characterized a commensal Escherichia coli ST156 isolate recovered from a clinically healthy companion dog in South Korea that carried blaNDM-5 and mcr-1 on distinct plasmids. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing revealed a multidrug-resistant phenotype, including resistance to carbapenems (imipenem MIC, ≥8 μg/mL) and colistin (MIC, 8 μg/mL). Hybrid long- and short-read genome assembly localized blaNDM-5 to an IncX3 plasmid and mcr-1 to an IncX4 plasmid. Broth-mating assays showed that each plasmid was independently transferable under the corresponding single-antimicrobial selection. Among 30 transconjugant colonies screened under each selection, both resistance determinants were detected in five colistin-selected and two meropenem-selected colonies, indicating co-detection of both resistance determinants in a minority of the screened colonies. Comparative genomic analysis showed that the IncX4-mcr-1 plasmid shared a highly conserved backbone with globally distributed IncX4 plasmids from diverse sources. These findings demonstrate asymptomatic carriage of independently transferable carbapenem- and colistin-resistance plasmids in a companion animal and support the inclusion of companion animals in integrated antimicrobial resistance surveillance.

title: Development of cinnamyl derivatives as antibiotic-potentiating agents.
abstract: Here, we report the discovery and optimization of 1-cinnamylpiperazine derivatives as antibiotic-potentiating agents inspired by the known RND efflux pump inhibitor 1-(1-naphthylmethyl)piperazine (NMP). A structurally diverse series of analogues was synthesized and evaluated for intrinsic antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity, and ability to potentiate antibiotic activity against Escherichia coli. Most derivatives showed low intrinsic antibacterial activity, consistent with an adjuvant mode of action. In combination assays, several compounds enhanced the antibiotic activity of erythromycin and linezolid, with halogenated derivatives showing the strongest potentiating effects. Compound 27 displayed the broadest potentiation profile, showing synergistic interactions with five of the seven tested antibiotics, namely linezolid, novobiocin, fusidic acid, pyridomycin, and clindamycin. Notably, it showed a superior potency to the structurally related reference inhibitor NMP. Experiments with AcrAB-TolC-deficient E. coli mutants, together with dye accumulation (Hoechst 33342) and membrane-permeabilization assays, suggested that 1-cinnamylpiperazine derivatives modulate efflux-associated resistance in a manner distinct from NMP, with increased membrane permeability likely contributing to their overall potentiating effect. Beyond planktonic cultures, compound 27 also potentiated erythromycin and linezolid against mature E. coli biofilms. These findings identify 1-cinnamylpiperazines as promising antibiotic adjuvant scaffolds for further optimization against drug-resistant Gram-negative infections.

title: Staphylococcus warneri MN336185 from Fermented Rice Water: a Multifunctional Probiotic with Anti-pathogenic and Longevity Benefits in C. elegans.
abstract: Fermented ecosystems serve as critical reservoirs for functionally diverse microorganisms with applications in food safety and nutraceuticals. This study focuses on Staphylococcus warneri MN336185 (SW), a non-traditional probiotic strain isolated from fermented rice water and evaluating its probiotic and bio-preservative properties. SW demonstrated significant gastrointestinal and oxidative stress tolerance, high epithelial cytocompatibility (> 80%), non-hemolytic safety, and an exceptional cholesterol assimilation efficiency of 85%. Moreover, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) confirmed genomic biosafety, establishing the absence of acquired enterotoxins, superantigens, ica-dependent biofilm determinants, and most transmissible antibiotic resistance elements. Studies on the host-microbe interface confirmed strong adherence of SW to HT-29 cells with proportionate competitive anti-adhesion potential against Salmonella enterica and Escherichia coli. The strain could also upregulate tight-junction proteins, claudins and zona occludens, indicating barrier-protective effects. In Caenorhabditis elegans, supplementation of SW as live feed enhanced lifespan, pharyngeal pumping, locomotory abilities, and resistance to pathogens. Further, challenge tests involving incorporation of live cells or cell-free supernatant of SW into rice-based matrices resulted in significant, time-dependent reduction of pathogens with a 4 log₁₀ CFU decrease during refrigerated storage. Collectively, these observations could establish S. warneri MN336185 as a multifunctional probiotic strain with potential application in functional food and natural biopreservation strategies.

title: Neonatal Sepsis in a Nigerian Tertiary Hospital: A 4 - Year Blood Culture - Based Analysis of Etiology, Resistance Patterns, and Preterm-Term Risk Factors.
abstract:
Background: Neonatal sepsis continues to be a significant cause of illness and death among neonates in developing countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where antimicrobial resistance complicates management.
Aim: The aim of the study is to determine the prevalence, bacterial etiologies, susceptibility patterns, and associated risk factors of laboratory-confirmed neonatal sepsis in a tertiary hospital in south-eastern Nigeria.
Methods: This retrospective observational study reviewed medical and laboratory databases of neonates admitted between January 2021 and December 2024. The blood culture method was BacT/ALERT system. Isolates were identified, and antibiotics sensitivity testing was done using standard methods. Data were analyzed using SPSS v25, and strength of associations tested by binary logistic regression at a significance level of P < 0.05.
Results: A total of 331 neonatal sepsis cases had blood cultures done and 105 (31.7%) had positive cultures. Early-onset sepsis accounted for 79% of cases, and 54.3% occurred in preterm neonates. Gram-negative isolates (51.4%) slightly predominated Gram-positives (48.6%). The leading pathogens were Staphylococcus aureus (28.6%), Klebsiella spp (18.1%), and Escherichia coli (13.3%). Gram-positives were most susceptible to clindamycin (83.3%), cefoxitin (75%), and amikacin (72.2%), while Gram-negatives showed the highest susceptibility to piperacillin/tazobactam (88.5%), meropenem (81.6%), and cefepime (71.8%). Ceftriaxone resistance was noted in 41% of Gram-negatives. Preterm neonates were significantly associated with Gram-negative infections (OR = 0.21, 95% CI: 0.09-0.48, P < 0.001).
Conclusion: Neonatal sepsis in this setting is common, with Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella spp , and Escherichia coli as major pathogens. The high level of resistance to 3 rd generation cephalosporins suggests the need to revise empirical treatment guidelines.

title: Shared Resistance, Phage-Receptor, and Biofilm Determinants in Antibiotic-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli, and Acinetobacter baumannii: A Bibliometric and Gene-Network Analysis of Phage Cocktail Research.
abstract:
Background/objectives: Antimicrobial resistance has renewed interest in bacteriophage cocktails as antibacterial and adjunctive agents, but the global research landscape and the bacterial determinants that constrain cocktail performance have not been mapped within a single framework. We quantified global phage-cocktail research and tested whether antibiotic-resistance, phage-receptor, and biofilm gene sets converge on shared genes in three Gram-negative pathogens representing three bacterial orders.
Methods: The Web of Science Core Collection was searched on 5 July 2026 (query "phage" and "cocktail"). After deduplication and screening, 1598 articles and reviews (1992-2026) were analyzed with bibliometric workflows, citation-burst and co-citation analyses, and a focused China-United States comparison. Because these are the two leading producers and represent the dominant biocontrol and clinical research models, the comparison is deliberately restricted to them and is not presented as a global ranking. Resistance (R), phage receptor/defense (P), and biofilm (B) gene sets were curated for Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1, Escherichia coli K-12, and Acinetobacter baumannii ATCC 17978; overlaps were tested by one-sided hypergeometric tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction and against size-matched control gene sets, followed by STRING protein-protein interaction and KEGG/GO enrichment. Orthologous conservation was assessed with KEGG Orthology in addition to gene-symbol matching.
Results: Annual output grew from 2 records (1992-1996) to 873 (2022-2026; 54.6% of the corpus), led by the USA (322 records) and China (292). Phage-receptor-biofilm overlaps were strongly enriched in all three species (29, 7, and 28 genes; odds ratios 47.0, 8.1, and 31.7; all P ≤ 7.6 × 10-5), whereas resistance-phage-receptor overlaps were strongly enriched in PAO1 (18 genes; odds ratio 17.7) and K-12 (26 genes; odds ratio 30.2) but not in A. baumannii (9 genes; odds ratio 1.8; P = 0.088). Four unrelated control gene sets showed no enrichment in any species (odds ratios 0-1.9; P ≥ 0.42). Candidate networks formed alginate, Psl-Pel, lipopolysaccharide-modification, and SOS/porin modules; KEGG enrichment converged on biofilm formation and cationic antimicrobial peptide resistance; 14 of the 18 symbol-level conserved genes were corroborated by shared KEGG Orthology assignments.
Conclusions: Phage-cocktail research has entered a phase of rapid growth, with hotspots converging on combination therapy and formulation. Biofilm-matrix synthesis and surface-appendage assembly form a transferable interface between phage adsorption and biofilm formation across three bacterial orders, whereas the coupling between antibiotic resistance and phage-receptor genes is lineage-restricted. Because the R, P, and B sets overlap by construction, these convergences are hypothesis-generating and require experimental validation before they can be used as design rules.

title: Whole-Genome Characterization of Pediatric Urinary E. coli Isolates from a Tertiary Care Pediatric Hospital in Guayaquil, Ecuador: Identification of the High-Risk ST1193 Clone.
abstract:
Background: Escherichia coli is a leading cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs) in children, and increasing antimicrobial resistance complicates empirical treatment. However, genomic information on pediatric urinary E. coli associated with urinary tract infection in Ecuador remains limited.
Objective: This exploratory study analyzed four E. coli isolates obtained from urine samples of pediatric patients at a tertiary hospital in Guayaquil, Ecuador.
Methods: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed to determine sequence types (STs), serotypes, antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) virulence factors (VFs), and phylogenetic relationships.
Results: Two isolates were assigned to the globally disseminated high-risk clone ST1193 and carried extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) genes, including blaCTX-M-27, whereas one isolate was assigned to ST162 and carried blaCTX-M-65. The remaining isolate could not be assigned to a complete ST because of missing MLST loci, but it harbored blaCTX-M-15, blaOXA-1, and blaTEM-1. Fluoroquinolone resistance-associated substitutions were detected in gyrA, parC, and parE in three isolates. The isolates shared a conserved set of VFs involved in adhesion, iron acquisition, and secretion systems. ARGs were frequently associated with insertion sequences and IncF plasmid replicons, indicating a potential contribution of mobile genetic elements (MGEs) to the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance.
Conclusions: Despite the limited number of isolates, these findings provide preliminary genomic evidence of the presence of ST1193 and diverse ESBL-producing urinary E. coli lineages among pediatric patients in Guayaquil, supporting the need for expanded genomic surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship efforts at the hospital level.

title: Divergent Organism-Specific Trajectories of Multidrug Resistance Across the COVID-19 Pandemic: An Interrupted Time-Series Study in a Mexican Tertiary Hospital, 2017-Early 2026.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Whether the COVID-19 pandemic uniformly increased antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is contested, and aggregate analyses may mask organism-specific patterns. The objective of the study was to characterize changes in the level and slope of monthly multidrug-resistant (MDR), possible extensively drug-resistant (pXDR), possible pandrug-resistant (pPDR), vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE), and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) positivity at a Mexican tertiary-care hospital, and to assess heterogeneity by organism, antimicrobial class, specimen type, and hospital service. Methods: Retrospective interrupted time-series of deduplicated bacterial isolates (October 2017 to January 2026), analyzed by segmented regression across pre-pandemic, pandemic, and post-peak phases. Results: Cohort-wide MDR positivity had been declining before 2020 and rose abruptly at pandemic onset (level shift +6.81 percentage points, p = 0.0092) with a simultaneous slope reversal, reaching 24.27 percentage points above the extrapolated pre-pandemic trend by February 2022 (95% CI 14.26-34.28, p < 0.0001). The decline resumed after the pandemic peak, but the two slope changes did not offset one another (joint p = 0.0064). pXDR and pPDR moved in the same direction (+8.93, p = 0.0233; +15.40, p = 0.0113). VRE showed no significant departure, whereas MRSA declined in every phase yet departed significantly from its extrapolated trajectory (+23.68, p = 0.0040). Among species, Escherichia coli showed the largest departure from its counterfactual (+48.82 percentage points, p < 0.0001) and Klebsiella pneumoniae had the largest abrupt level rise (+14.46 percentage points, p = 0.0055), while S. aureus declined in every phase despite an abrupt rise in level at pandemic onset. At the class level, carbapenem and third-/fourth-generation cephalosporin non-susceptibility rose at pandemic onset and returned to baseline afterwards (19.1% to 28.0% to 18.7%, and 51.7% to 59.4% to 52.5%; all q < 0.001), whereas fluoroquinolone non-susceptibility rose and did not revert, climbing further in E. coli (61.5% to 65.2% to 72.7%, q = 0.0012) and plateauing at an elevated level in K. pneumoniae (37.6% to 46.5% to 49.3%, q = 0.1919 post-peak). Conclusions: Resistance trajectories across pandemic-related phases were divergent and, for the Gram-negative organisms, incompletely reversed, with the highest burden of advanced resistance in high-intensity settings. Organism-resolved surveillance and sustained stewardship are needed.

title: Screening, Mechanistic Investigation, and In Vivo Efficacy of a Compound Chinese Herbal Formulation Against Bovine-Derived Escherichia coli K99.
abstract: Background:Escherichia coli (E. coli) K99 is one of the major pathogens responsible for neonatal calf diarrhea, characterized by widespread transmission and strong pathogenicity, leading to high mortality in calves and substantial economic losses in the cattle industry. Antibiotic-based therapies are increasingly challenged by drug residues and continuous emergence of antimicrobial resistance, which creates an urgent demand for safe and effective alternative antimicrobial agents. Chinese herbal medicines (CHMs), featuring low toxicity, abundant resources and synergistic effects of multiple bioactive constituents, have become promising candidates for new antibacterial agents. Objectives: This study aimed to screen Chinese herbal medicines for antibacterial activity against bovine-derived E. coli K99-2, develop a compound herbal formula F1 following the traditional "Jun-Chen-Zuo-Shi" compatibility principle, and systematically characterize its chemical composition, antibacterial mechanism, in-vivo safety and protective therapeutic efficacy. Materials and Methods: Seventy Chinese herbal medicines were subjected to in-vitro antibacterial screening using the Oxford cup agar diffusion assay. Candidate compound formulas were designed according to screening outcomes and "Jun-Chen-Zuo-Shi" theory. The MIC and MBC of the optimized formula F1 were determined via broth microdilution. LC-MS was performed to profile chemical constituents of F1. Growth curves, membrane potential, cell-wall permeability, intracellular protein and ATP levels, gel retardation assay and scanning electron microscopy were applied to investigate antibacterial mechanisms. A 28-day repeated oral gavage toxicity test in Kunming mice was conducted to evaluate biosafety. The LD50 of E. coli K99-2 was determined by intraperitoneal challenge, and a mouse infection model was used to assess the in-vivo protective effect of F1. Results:Fructus Mume and Cornus officinalis displayed prominent antibacterial activity against K99-2. The optimized compound formula F1 produced an inhibition-zone diameter of 21 mm; both MIC and MBC were 62.5 mg/mL. Putatively annotated constituents of F1 included furan derivatives, amino acids, flavonoids, polyphenolic compounds and organic acids. F1 triggered bacterial cell-envelope damage, membrane depolarization, reduction of intracellular protein content and disturbance of ATP-associated energy metabolism, while it did not form stable complexes with bacterial genomic DNA. The 28-day oral toxicity assay revealed no obvious toxic manifestations within the tested dose range in mice. In the K99-2 infection-challenge experiment, oral administration of F1 raised the mouse survival rate from 40% (untreated infected control) to 73%. Discussion: Compound herbal formula F1 exerts multi-target antibacterial activity against E. coli K99-2 mainly by disrupting bacterial structural integrity and interfering with energy metabolism rather than directly binding to genomic DNA. F1 demonstrates favorable preliminary biosafety and can improve survival of K99-2-infected mice, indicating its potential as a veterinary herbal candidate for prevention and control of calf diarrhea caused by E. coli K99. Further work is required to identify key bioactive components, optimize dosage and verify efficacy in calf clinical settings. This research provides experimental basis for developing antimicrobial herbal veterinary preparations.

title: Carbapenem and Multidrug Resistance Among Gram-Negative Bacilli in a County Emergency Clinical Hospital from Western Romania: A Retrospective Study, 2024-2025.
abstract: Background and Objectives: Antimicrobial resistance among Gram-negative bacilli is a major clinical challenge, particularly in hospitals where carbapenem-resistant and multidrug-resistant organisms limit therapeutic options. This study aimed to characterize the distribution and resistance profiles of Gram-negative bacilli isolated in a university-affiliated hospital in western Romania during 2024-2025, focusing on temporal variation, intensive care unit (ICU) origin, carbapenem resistance, and multidrug resistance (MDR). Materials and Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included 8931 Gram-negative isolates recovered from clinical specimens between January 2024 and December 2025. Bacterial identification was performed using the VITEK 2 Compact system and/or MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, whereas antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the VITEK 2 system and interpreted according to EUCAST criteria. Carbapenem resistance was defined as resistance to meropenem, imipenem, or ertapenem for Enterobacterales and to meropenem or imipenem for Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii. MDR was defined as resistance to at least one agent in at least three antimicrobial classes. Factors associated with MDR were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression. Results: Escherichia coli was the most frequent isolate (36.0%), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae (22.8%), P. aeruginosa (9.6%), A. baumannii (9.4%), and Proteus mirabilis (8.0%). Among 8708 isolates evaluable for both outcomes, carbapenem resistance was 30.8% and MDR was 44.5%; both were significantly more frequent in 2025 than in 2024. ICU isolates showed higher carbapenem resistance (56.1% vs. 18.0%) and MDR (65.3% vs. 33.9%) than non-ICU isolates. A. baumannii had the highest burden, with 87.4% carbapenem resistance and 87.5% MDR. MDR was independently associated with study year, ICU origin, age group, sex, specimen type, and bacterial species; the strongest association was observed for A. baumannii versus E. coli (adjusted OR 23.45, 95% CI 18.38-29.91). Conclusions: Carbapenem resistance and MDR were frequent, particularly among ICU isolates and high-risk pathogens. The findings support intensified local surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, and targeted infection prevention and control measures.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance in E. coli and Salmonella spp. Across Romanian Animal-Food-Environment Interfaces: Current Evidence and One Health Knowledge Gaps.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an important One Health challenge, yet evidence on resistant Escherichia coli and Salmonella spp. in Romania is dispersed across animal species, food matrices, environmental compartments, and surveillance systems. This comprehensive narrative review synthesizes and critically evaluates evidence across animal-food-environment interfaces and places it in the context of broader European AMR patterns. Particular attention is given to isolate origin, resistance phenotypes, multidrug resistance, major resistance determinants, molecular epidemiology, and the strength of evidence supporting cross-sector connections. Studies most frequently addressed poultry and swine, where resistance to ampicillin, fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, and tetracyclines was repeatedly reported, together with extended-spectrum cephalosporin resistance, particularly in E. coli. Evidence from cattle, foods of animal origin, companion animals, wildlife, wastewater, and aquatic environments shows that resistant bacteria and antimicrobial resistance genes occur across multiple compartments. Substantial heterogeneity in sampling design, susceptibility testing, and molecular characterization limits direct comparison between studies, while epidemiologically linked investigations and whole-genome sequencing across connected reservoirs remain uncommon. Priorities include more standardized cross-sector surveillance, stronger environmental monitoring, expanded genomic epidemiology, improved data interoperability, and continued antimicrobial stewardship. By integrating fragmented national evidence, this review identifies both well-characterized sectors and interfaces where important evidence gaps remain.

title: Distribution and Antimicrobial Resistance Patterns of Critical and High-Priority Gram-Negative Pathogens Isolated from Endotracheal Aspirates in an Intensive Care Unit.
abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections represent the world's deadliest infectious disease, responsible for approximately 2.5 million deaths worldwide. The aim of the study was to determine the distribution and antimicrobial susceptibility profiles of the main critical and high priority Gram-negative bacteria isolated from endotracheal aspirates obtained from Intensive Care Unit (ICU) patients. We conducted a four-year microbiological surveillance study (2022-2025) in a tertiary Romanian ICU. A total of 1529 Gram-negative bacterial isolates were detected in 1391 endotracheal aspirates. Most frequently reported were Pseudomonas aeruginosa (422-27.60%), Acinetobacter baumannii (296-19.36%), Escherichia coli (274-17.92%) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (271-17.73%). The prevalence of MDR Acinetobacter baumannii declined to approximately 40% in 2025, whereas XDR isolates increased to 13.51%, twice the 2022 value. Carbapenem resistance among Acinetobacter baumannii remained high (around 70%) in 2025, despite a significant decline from 2022 (p < 0.001). Approximately 65% of K. pneumoniae isolates were MDR/XDR, with an increase in carbapenem resistance. MDR Pseudomonas aeruginosa increased significantly from 14.14% in 2022 to 39.84% in 2025 (p < 0.001) and a significant upward trend in carbapenem resistance was registered, exceeding 70% for imipenem in 2025. These findings underscore the need for continuous microbiological and epidemiological surveillance and targeted interventions to prevent the spread of highly resistant pathogens.

title: DNA defense systems become a fitness liability during plasmid conjugation.
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer via conjugative plasmids is a major driver of bacterial evolution. While antibiotic exposure selects for the resistance genes carried by some plasmids, much uncertainty remains about how plasmids persist and spread in microbial communities in the absence of such external selection. Here, we show that conjugative plasmid transfer selectively reduces the fitness of non-permissive recipients through the process of lethal zygosis: a phenomenon in which repeated Type IV Secretion System (T4SS) engagement damages recipients that fail to establish the plasmid. We found that this contact-dependent antagonism effectively clears a niche for plasmid donors by turning recipients' DNA defenses into a liability. Blocking establishment of the plasmid RK2 with CRISPR-Cas or restriction-modification caused strong fitness defects in Escherichia coli recipients by preventing expression of plasmid-encoded exclusion genes and leaving cells exposed to repeated T4SS engagement. We leveraged this insight to resolve an obstacle in bacterial editing by developing transposon vectors that co-deliver exclusion genes, increasing the efficiency of gene editing by orders of magnitude. Our results reveal the role of "coercive assimilation" in horizontal gene transfer, exposing a tradeoff where the advantage of bacterial immunity to foreign DNA is counterbalanced by increased susceptibility to lethal zygosis.

title: Genomic characterization of ESBL-producing Escherichia coli isolates from patients in an orthopaedic ward in Mwanza, Tanzania.
abstract:
Background: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli are a major contributor to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in healthcare settings, yet their genomic diversity and population structure remain poorly characterized in low-resource settings. Orthopaedic wards may facilitate persistence, acquisition, and possible onward spread of resistant organisms due to prolonged hospitalization, frequent antimicrobial exposure, and increased patient vulnerability. This study investigated the genomic characteristics of ESBL-producing E. coli recovered from hospitalized patients in an orthopaedic ward in Mwanza, Tanzania.
Methods: We performed whole-genome sequencing and comparative genomic analysis of ESBL-confirmed E. coli isolates obtained from stool or rectal swabs of hospitalized patients. Sequence reads were quality controlled and assembled using standard pipelines. Core genome single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) alignments were generated using Snippy, and recombination was identified and masked using Gubbins prior to phylogenetic reconstruction. Sequence types (STs), phylogroups, predicted serotypes, putative pathotype-associated marker profiles, AMR determinants, plasmid replicons, and virulence-associated genes were identified using established bioinformatics tools and databases.
Results: Phylogenetic analysis revealed a polyclonal population structure comprising multiple distinct lineages rather than a single outbreak clone. Several isolates formed low-SNP clusters compatible with recent shared ancestry, possible shared-source exposure, or localized circulation within the ward. The population included internationally recognized sequence types, including ST131, ST1193, ST69, ST617, and ST38. Phylogroup analysis showed a diverse distribution, with phylogroup A most common, followed by B1, B2, D, U/unassigned, C, F, and one cryptic lineage. ESBL production was predominantly associated with bla CTX-M-15, detected in most isolates, alongside additional resistance determinants to aminoglycosides, quinolones, sulfonamides, trimethoprim, and tetracyclines. IncF-family plasmid replicons predominated, with additional IncY plasmids identified. Virulence-associated genes, including fdeC and ybtP/ybtQ, were widely distributed.
Conclusions: ESBL-producing E. coli in this orthopaedic ward represent a genomically diverse, multidrug-resistant population dominated by bla CTX-M-15-positive lineages. The coexistence of multiple lineages alongside low-SNP clusters suggests repeated introductions with possible localized circulation; however, genomic similarity alone cannot establish direct transmission. These findings highlight colonized patients as reservoirs of AMR and underscore the need to integrate genomic surveillance into infection prevention and control strategies in resource-constrained healthcare settings.

title: Plasmid-Mediated AmpC Detection in Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae: In Vitro Prevalence and In Silico Inhibitor Design.
abstract:
Objectives: This study investigated the prevalence of AmpC beta-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae in clinical specimens collected in Lahore, Pakistan, and aimed to identify potential inhibitors targeting AmpC beta-lactamases.
Methods: A total of 17,500 clinical specimens were collected from June 2018 to June 2021 and analyzed for E. coli and K. pneumoniae. These isolates underwent phenotypic identification using microscopy and the API 20E kit. AmpC beta-lactamase production was initially screened using cefoxitin disk diffusion and inhibitor-based methods, while the presence of plasmid-borne AmpC genes (CIT, EBC, and DHA) was confirmed by PCR. Additionally, the study used computational drug discovery techniques to screen for oxadiazole, quinazolinone, and sulfonylurea derivatives as potential inhibitors of the AmpC protein.
Results: Our data showed high antibiotic resistance rates among E. coli and K. pneumoniae isolates: 74.5% were resistant to cefotaxime and ceftazidime, and 45% to cefoxitin. PCR testing revealed that the CIT gene was the most prevalent in both E. coli (65.4%) and K. pneumoniae (63%), while other genes (EBC and DHA) and combinations were also present (p < 0.005). Using computational drug discovery, several compound libraries were screened against the AmpC protein. Tolbutamide showed the most promising results, with strong binding affinity and favorable drug-like properties.
Conclusion: Plasmid-mediated AmpC beta-lactamase-producing E. coli and K. pneumoniae were highly prevalent, with the CIT genotype predominating among clinical isolates. Computational screening identified Tolbutamide as a promising lead compound, warranting further experimental validation before therapeutic application.
journal: The Canadian journal of infectious diseases & medical microbiology = Journal canadien des maladies infectieuses et de la microbiologie medicale

title: The burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in the WHO Western Pacific Region 1990-2021: a cross-country systematic analysis with forecasts to 2050.
abstract:
Background: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most significant challenges to global health. Although reports from the WHO Western Pacific Region (WPR) increasingly recognise the implications of AMR, precise estimates of the problem's extent remain limited. We present a comprehensive time-trend analysis of AMR burden in the WPR between 1990 and 2021, with forecasts to 2050.
Methods: Using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study 2021 methods, we estimated deaths and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) attributable to and associated with AMR across 11 infectious syndromes, 22 bacterial pathogens, and 84 pathogen-drug combinations for the WPR and its constituent countries. Data were drawn from mortality registries, surveillance platforms, hospital records, and systematic reviews. The modelling framework comprised five key components: estimation of deaths in which infection had a role, the proportion of infectious deaths attributable to specific syndromes, allocation of syndrome-specific deaths to individual pathogens, the percentage of a given pathogen resistant to an antimicrobial drug of interest, and quantification of the excess mortality risk or prolonged infection duration associated with resistance. Burden was then estimated under two counterfactual scenarios: AMR-attributable (resistant infections replaced by susceptible ones) and AMR-associated (infections prevented altogether). Country-level estimates and forecasts to 2050 were generated using predictive statistical models, with uncertainty reported as 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs).
Findings: In 2021, we estimated 1,150,000 deaths (95% UI 1,000,000-1,290,000) associated with bacterial AMR and 248,000 deaths (215,000-281,000) attributable to bacterial AMR across 32 WPR locations. Between 1990 and 2021, deaths in children under 5 dropped by 87.3%, while deaths in adults 70 and older rose by 88.9%. Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Escherichia coli accounted for over 50% of AMR deaths. The Solomon Islands and Kiribati had the highest age-standardised mortality rates; New Zealand had the lowest burden in 2021. By 2050, associated and attributable deaths could reach 1,840,000 (1,460,000-2,230,000) and 402,000 (322,000-480,000), respectively.
Interpretation: The WPR contributes substantially to global AMR burden, with considerable fatal and non-fatal impact from key resistant pathogens. Despite data limitations, these estimates support informed decision-making regarding resource allocation and funding-emphasising the need for collaborative, multi-sectoral action against AMR.
Funding: Wellcome Trust, and the UK Department of Health and Social Care using aid funding managed by the Fleming Fund.
journal: The Lancet regional health. Western Pacific

title: Rv0783c of Mycobacterium tuberculosis Acts as a Proton-Motive Force Dependent Multidrug Efflux Transporter Involved in the Efflux of Structurally Unrelated Antibiotics and Enhancing Biofilm Formation.
abstract: Despite multiple treatment strategies and extensive research on resistance mechanisms, tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health concern, largely because of the rise of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB. Among various mechanisms complicating the situation, active antibiotic export via efflux pumps is particularly significant, yet largely unexplored. Mycobacterium sp. encodes numerous transporters, many of which are overexpressed in clinical isolates or under drug stress. Here, we examined the possible role of Rv0783c, a putative transporter that is reportedly overexpressed in drug-stressed conditions. Rv0783c conferred resistance to multiple structurally diverse antibiotics, fluoroquinolones and anti-TB drugs in the heterologous hosts, namely, Escherichia coli and Mycobacterium smegmatis. Reduced drug accumulation and active efflux of ethidium bromide (EtBr) confirmed its transport activity, which in turn gets nullified upon using the proton-motive force blocker, CCCP (Carbonyl Cyanide m-Chlorophenylhydrazone). On the other hand, its expression enhanced biofilm formation, linking antibiotic resistance to persistence-associated phenotype. Furthermore, site-directed mutagenesis confirmed the presence of crucial interacting residues with antibiotics that were identified by in silico analysis. Overall, we demonstrate the role of Rv0783c in the extrusion of first and second-line anti-TB drugs and enhancing biofilm formation.

title: Genetic architecture and transmission potential of the blaTEM-1-associated resistance module in ST469 Salmonella Rissen.
abstract: Salmonella Rissen is an important foodborne non-typhoidal Salmonella pathogen; however, the antimicrobial resistance genetic characteristics of its ST469 lineage and the genetic basis underlying the dissemination of blaTEM-1-associated resistance regions remain poorly understood. In this study, three clinical isolates and 17 publicly available genomes were analyzed using phylogenetic analysis, core-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis, antimicrobial resistance gene profiling, mobile genetic element characterization, and source-stratified analysis, together with conjugation assays, long-read sequencing, characterization of the local genetic environment of blaTEM-1, and detection of outer membrane vesicle (OMV)-associated DNA to assess their transmission potential. The results showed that all three clinical isolates clustered within the ST469 phylogenetic background, with pairwise core-genome SNP differences ranging from 8 to 170 among the 20 isolates. Antimicrobial resistance gene profiles and mobile genetic element compositions exhibited inter-strain heterogeneity among isolates from different sources, but no clear source-specific patterns were observed. All three clinical isolates carried blaTEM-1, which was located within a local genetic region containing Tn1331 and other transposition-associated elements. Conjugation assays showed that blaTEM-1-associated genetic material could be transferred into the Escherichia coli J53 recipient strain. Long-read genomic analysis identified no plasmids directly carrying blaTEM-1 in any of the three donor strains. MobileElementFinder detected no integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs), and blaTEM-1 did not colocalize with any predicted prophage region. Further analysis showed that blaTEM-1-associated DNA remained detectable in purified GD29-derived OMVs after DNase I treatment, and its local genetic structure was highly consistent with the corresponding region in the donor strain. Collectively, ST469 Salmonella Rissen exhibited heterogeneous antimicrobial resistance genetic backgrounds, and the blaTEM-1-associated region demonstrated the capacity for intercellular transfer; in the absence of identifiable classical genetic vehicles that could explain this transfer, OMV-associated blaTEM-1 DNA provides indirect evidence supporting OMV-mediated noncanonical transfer of antimicrobial resistance genes. This study provides a basis for risk assessment of key antimicrobial resistance modules in ST469 Salmonella Rissen and for antimicrobial resistance surveillance in the context of food safety.
